newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Lebed calls for new elections in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Lebed calls for new elections in Russia.

text.p: Russian presidential hopeful General Alexander Lebed on Tuesday called for new elections in his country, which he said was teetering on the brink of disaster.

Referring to President Boris Yeltsin, who has been in poor health since before his re-election last year, Lebed said: "As a Christian one should wish him the speediest recovery ... but we have no time ...

"The presidential health drama is turning into a national tragedy," he told a packed news conference at U.N. headquarters after attending President Bill Clinton's inauguration in Washington on Monday as the guest of a U.S. congressman.

Lebed, who came a strong third in a presidential election last June and briefly served as Yeltsin's security adviser, has made it clear previously that he believes Yeltsin should quit because of his continuing ill health and allow a new election.

"If all the crises existing in Russia today merged into one, as is being forecast ... the country will start falling apart and different regions will be orienting themselves toward different allies." Some would look toward the United States and others toward Germany, Turkey, Finland or China, he said.
Speaking through an interpreter, he said such a collapse would result in the redivision of the world and then a new world war without victors.
"That is exactly what I want and wish to prevent," he said, urging Yeltsin to assess whether he could govern the country and, if not, "organize presidential elections ahead of time."

In an interview with CBS News, Lebed said he was not sure there would be elections in Russia should Yeltsin die because the "oligarchy ruling Russia does not want election." He said there was the "harsh possibility" that a state of emergency could be clamped instead.
Lebed began his hour-long news conference at the United Nations by quoting at length from a work by the late poet Vladimir Vysotsky which he said depicted Russia's current plight:
"....What we eat is just grass. Our souls have grown sour and pimples have come on our faces. And we've been solacing our souls too often with wine..."
"A great number of people are sick and tired of that. So am I," Lebed said. "I want to build another Russia -- a free democratic Russia that would be pleasant to deal with, trade with, visit."
He also proposed a "unilateral declaration by Russia of its adherence to peace ... Never again will a Russian soldier be on anybody's land as an occupier."

Asked by a Japanese reporter about the vexed question of the Kurile islands, occupied by Russia since the end of the Second World War, he shot back: "The Japanese, no matter what continent you meet them (on), start with the islands.
"Russia is a huge market. You should really be in a hurry to be there. And as a consolation you'll get four islands."

He told another questioner he did not consider that Russia was still a super-power. "If you are sitting in a muddy pond or pool, the first rule is not to make noises about how great you are. It wouldn't look right."

Questioned about possible NATO membership for a number of East European countries, Lebed said: "I take that very calmly, without any emotions or hysteria." But was the aim to "caress the ego of the victors in the Cold War or create a European or universal security system?" he asked.

The first option would mean that the "time for common sense to reign in the planet has not come yet," he said, suggesting NATO should change its role and tackle such problems as terrorism and drugs and conduct peacekeeping operations.
"It wouldn't be bad to change the label as well," he added, suggesting that in the minds of millions of people NATO "stands for fragments of the Cold War."
